title: Kuf

segments.voice: Yesterday, tzadi, and Noah, righteous in his generations. Your line: tzadi for tzaddik. Today, the letter that begins holy.

"Ye shall be holy: for I the LORD your God am holy." That's how Leviticus nineteen begins, in the King James words. It sounds like the start of something about temples and altars. There's an offering or two, but mostly something else. The same chapter tells you to leave the corners of your field for the poor, to pay a worker before the night is out, not to curse the deaf or trip the blind, to love your neighbor as yourself. Holiness, here, shows up at the edge of a field and on payday.
screen: `YE SHALL BE HOLY.` → `THE CORNERS OF THE FIELD.` → `PAY THE WORKER TONIGHT.`

segments.voice: Kuf makes a k sound, deep in the back of the mouth, and it begins kadosh, holy. Four steps. First, the root. Kadosh carries the sense of set apart, marked off for something. Holy things in Hebrew aren't necessarily shiny. They are distinct, given a different use. Second, a day. Early in Genesis, God rests on the seventh day, and in the King James words, "God blessed the seventh day, and sanctified it." Sanctified is the same root. Before the story has a sanctuary or a priest, it has a holy day. Jews meet that root on Friday night in kiddush, the blessing over wine that sets Shabbat apart. Third, a cry. Isaiah sees angels calling to one another, "Holy, holy, holy, is the LORD of hosts: the whole earth is full of his glory." Jews say those words in the Kedushah, a part of the service whose name means holiness, some rising on their toes as they say them. Fourth, the hands. Leviticus nineteen, which opens with be holy, fills itself with ordinary acts: fair weights, honest wages, respect for the old. Kiddush, Kaddish, Kedushah, kadosh: one letter and root run through wine, mourning, prayer and law. Holiness isn't kept on a mountain. It's set apart inside a field, a market, a workday. In this reading, something becomes holy when it's given a purpose beyond itself and treated that way.
screen: `KADOSH: SET APART.` · `A DAY MADE HOLY.` · `HOLY, HOLY, HOLY IN THE KEDUSHAH.` · `HOLINESS AT THE EDGE OF A FIELD.` · then, large: `YE SHALL BE HOLY.`

segments.voice: Think back over the last day and look for one moment that felt set apart, even slightly: the first sip of coffee in a quiet kitchen, a child's hand in yours, a fair deal honestly made, a stranger who held a door. It doesn't need to be religious to count. Hold it for a few breaths and ask what made it different from the minutes around it; if you pray, you can give thanks for it.
Kuf. The letter of kadosh, holy, and of kiddush and Kedushah: set apart for a purpose. Today's word.
Your line: kuf for kadosh. Holy means set apart, not far away. Rest well.

howItsDone: Jews say the words of Isaiah 6:3 in the Kedushah during the repetition of the Amidah, and make kiddush over wine to set Shabbat apart; Leviticus 19, which opens with "be holy", is read in the yearly Torah cycle.

chat.says: Isn't holiness just about temples and prayer? What does it have to do with work?
options: Leviticus 19 says be holy, then lists honest wages, fair weights and the field's corners.
Holy means shiny and perfect, so only temples and altars can really be holy.
Holy means set apart, so it belongs in prayer and stays away from ordinary work.
